newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN Council fails to agree on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: UN Council fails to agree on Iraq.

text.p: A week after Iraqi troops went on the offensive against Kurds, the U.N. Security Council was unable to take a common position on Baghdad's action that unleashed U.S. cruise missile attacks.

The council expects to discuss a British-drafted resolution again on Friday after Russian envoys consult with Moscow over new compromise language. "A final effort is being made to find an agreement," said Britain's Stephen Gomersall.

The deadlock illustrates the crumbling of the coalition that backed Washington in the Gulf War, with the United States coming under increasing criticism for firing cruise missiles against Iraq and then claiming it had U.N. authorisation to do so. Britain, however, remains a strong supporter.

For the past 24 hours Russia has opposed and even threatened to veto the resolution, which was watered down considerably in rapping Iraq for going into the Kurdish north. China agreed with Russia and France had some reservations, as did Egypt and Indonesia.

"What is the point of the resolution?," said Russian ambassador Sergei Lavrov, noting the United States had accomplished its mission in two air strikes in response to Baghdad's attack on the Kurdish city of Arbil.
Earlier Russia's deputy foreign minister said in Moscow that the resolution was an attempt to give legal underpinnings to the U.S. military actions against Iraq.
Any direct or veiled reference to the United States response to President Saddam Hussein's troops is missing from the resolution.
The latest British draft expresses "grave concern" rather than condemning operations by Baghdad's troops and calls for full and immediate withdrawal by Iraqi forces.
At the insistence of France, Italy and other members, the draft also leaves implementation of an oil-for-food deal for Iraq up to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, "when conditions permit."

An earlier version of the draft contained some conditions for the implementation of the plan that allows Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil to purhcase food and other goods for the Iraqi people suffering under six years of trade sanctions.
Boutros Boutros-Ghali last weekend put the plan on hold, saying he feared for the safety of U.N. personnel.

Many of the relief goods were to be distributed by the United Nations in the Kurdish city of Arbil. But the new shaky alliance between Iraq and one Kurdish party, which invited in Iraqi troops, means key elements of the programme have to be re-evaluated.
Egypt's veteran ambassador, Nabil Elaraby, said the resolution, in effect, was condemning Iraq for invading its own territory and "did not take into consideration that it was a sovereign country."
He said the resolution implied some kind of division of Iraq which his government "was very much concerned about and which we are very much against."
Elaraby said he was not justifying the Iraqi action, but laying out principles of how to deal with it.
The three northern provinces have been under allied protection since the end of the Gulf War, when President Saddam Hussein put down a rebellion and strafed fleeing Kurdish civilians from the air.
